lines.note: Hito ja closes a Japanese example continued from the preceding page. The Portuguese characterizes the person as very imprudent; this is a continuation, not a new headword.
Mufunkyoo concerns an inappropriate or brusque reply. The complete initial M is visible at the ordinary headword size and restores the letter omitted by OCR; fora continues into de propoſito below.
Completes the definition as answering off the point and harshly. The example begins the adjectival form Mufunqiô-na, divided with a visible line-end hyphen.

The example prohibits saying such inappropriate things; navoxerareſo is the printed prohibitive expression, not the stale kana hint's modern-looking verb. The Portuguese translation begins 'do not say absurdities'; its final des- has a hyphen, not the OCR period.
Completes des-propoſitos, the inappropriate or nonsensical remarks prohibited above. The t is present in the scan and was omitted by OCR.

runs.text: O não ter estudado, ou não ſaber letras.

lines.note: Mugaku denotes lack of study or literacy. The gloss distinguishes not having studied from not knowing letters; its historical spelling is not modernized.
Mugakuna is the adjectival form, here applied to an unlettered, uneducated person. It is a separate printed entry, not another principal part of a verb.
Mugai is glossed as something without boundary or measure. This sense, rather than an unrelated modern homophone, determines the reading in context.

runs.text: Couſa que não tem termo, como mar

lines.note: Mugaitei likewise denotes boundlessness. The sea is introduced as the comparison and the descriptive phrase continues on the following row.
Completes the comparison with the immense sea. The final upright S. is the dictionary's written-language label, separate from the italic Portuguese gloss.
Mugan is explained by manako nashi, having no eyes, and glossed as blind. Both Japanese expressions are roman; Cego is the Portuguese equivalent.
Mugana hito introduces a person with little spirit or concern. The abbreviation Homẽ is retained, and pou continues into co without supplying a hyphen absent at the right edge.

runs.text: co brio, ou eſpiritos, ou que não ſe lhe dà das

lines.note: Completes pouco brio and describes someone lacking spirit or indifferent to things. The reflexive ſe, not OCR fe, is supported by the scan and the Portuguese expression não ſe lhe dà.
Couſas completes the expression for not caring about things. This short continuation belongs to Mugana rather than the following Buddhist entry.

runs.text: Neſcio, ou idiota nas couſas do

lines.note: Mugansu is first someone ignorant of the religious matters named below. The scan has idiota, not OCR iliota; the additional sense of illiteracy follows after the paragraph sign.

runs.text: Buppô, ou Satori. ¶ Item, Homem que

lines.note: Buppô and Satori name Buddhist teaching and awakening within the Portuguese explanation. Enlarged type comparison supports italic printing for both complete terms, correcting the OCR's isolated roman B. The mark over Buppô is a circumflex; the next sense starts 'a person who'.
Completes the second Muganſu sense: someone unable to read or write. The abbreviation nẽ is retained rather than expanded to modern nem.
Muji and mujina describe plain, undecorated metal or gold. Gi naxi is the Japanese explanatory expression; l introduces the alternative adjectival form.
The metal lacks relief work or moulding. This completes the material, decorative sense of Mugi, distinct from the barley entry later in the column.
Mujuusho is explained as having nowhere to live. The narrow, worn vowel and its mark are retained as iǔ from the aligned reading; the Portuguese lu- begins lugar.
Completes lugar de habitação, a place of residence. Upright S. labels the expression as written usage, not as part of the italic definition.
Mugon, literally without words, means silence. Mu- starts the repeated headword in the verbal example on the following row.
Mugon suru is to remain silent or not speak. The divided Japanese example and its two Portuguese paraphrases stay on their physical rows.
Muguu is explained by kiwamari nashi, without limit. The Portuguese alternative begins 'without boundary or' and continues below.
Completes the definition with 'end', then gives saying or doing interminable things. The carons in Mugǔna and yǔ are retained, and l means 'or', not a Japanese syllable.

runs.text: Dizer, ou fazer couſas que não tem fin, nem

lines.note: Translates the preceding example as saying or doing things without end or conclusion. The damaged i of Dizer is retained contextually; the scan supports historical fin rather than silently substituting fim.
Concluſão completes 'neither end nor conclusion'. Its l, not OCR i, is supported by the tall stroke and the Portuguese noun.
Muge here means unobstructed, explained by sawari nashi and 'without hindrance'. The separate written-language label S. is upright.
This homonymous Mugue means priceless or beyond valuation, as atai nashi makes clear. The printed line break divides the Portuguese inestimauel.
The example describes priceless treasure, translated as riches. The visibly unusual xijfô is retained rather than regularized to an expected modern or historical spelling solely from meaning.
The riches have great, inestimable value. The scan lacks the extra n in OCR ineſtimnauel; the tight printed joining to preço is retained, and S. remains a separate roman label.
Mugen is explained by yume and maboroshi, dreams and apparitions. The Portuguese begins a comparison with light, fleeting dreams, completed on the next row.

runs.text: & breues. Tomaſe por couſas breues, & que

lines.note: The dreams are brief; the expression is extended to transient things generally. The relative clause continues with their quickly passing away on the next row.

Completes the description of things that soon pass. Muguen fǒyǒ supplies a synonymous expression for transience. The second ſ of paſſão is heavily abraded: enlargement reveals residual strokes in its position, supporting the doubled reading rather than silently normalizing solely from Portuguese spelling.
Mugena describes something miserable or pitiable. Its meaning is not the same as the preceding dream-and-illusion noun despite the similar spelling.
Mugeni is the adverbial form, glossed with miserable and pitiable circumstances. The Portuguese compaßiuamente is divided after compaßi-.
Completes the adverbial gloss and adds 'without reason'. The example begins mugeni korosareta, with the verb divided at co-.
Korosareta is the passive past: the person was killed. The Portuguese says they killed him unjustifiably and cruelly; its historical attached pronoun in Matarãono is preserved.
Completes the account of the killing as occurring miserably or pitifully. It is a short continuation of the translation, not an independent adverb entry.
Mugetsukenai denotes something cruel or inhuman. The Portuguese confirms the harsher sense of this form, rather than merely pitiful circumstances.
Mugetsukenoo is the adverb corresponding to Mugetsukenai. The printed caron is retained, and the following example illustrates doing something cruelly.
The example means killing many people cruelly. Coroite is an historical i-onbin form of the s-row verb, not a reason to insert the syllable of modern koroshite.

runs.text: Matando a muitos homẽs ſem piedade.

lines.note: The Portuguese explicitly translates the act as killing many people without mercy. Homẽs keeps the printed abbreviation rather than spelling out homens.
Mugi covers wheat or barley in this gloss. Its gui spelling distinguishes it from the earlier Mugi meaning plain or undecorated.
Mugi ii is barley cooked like rice. The separate iy represents the food noun, not a stray letter or the beginning of the next line.
The example means preparing or cooking the barley food. A visible paragraph sign omitted by OCR has been restored; ar- begins arroz on the following row.
Completes arroz de ceuada, literally barley 'rice'. This is the final body row of the left column, with the lower rule safely outside its text.
Mugyoo means without shape, explained by katachi nashi. The example introduced by italic Vt follows on the next physical line.
Mushiki mugyoo is rendered as something without colour or form. The caron in muguiǒ is visible and the abbreviation nẽ is not expanded.
Muguu jizai describes complete freedom without limit. The first element repeats the boundlessness vocabulary of the left column.

Mugura, or preferably Muguramochi, names a mole. The r after Mugu has a surviving stem but a badly worn shoulder; the adjacent Mugura and the lack of an i-dot support r rather than OCR Mugui amochi. The letter is not simply omitted. Potiùs is an italic Latin editorial word.
Mu-i is without rank or dignity, explained by kurai nashi. Its internal hyphen is genuinely printed and is not a line-end division to remove.
Muquan completes mu-i, muquan, the paired expression for lacking rank and office. Idem refers back to the same Portuguese meaning.
Muichimotsu means not even one thing. The printed final t is the historical checked ending, not an omitted tçu; the final S. is an upright written-usage label.
Mujin is explained as never coming to an end. The Portuguese begins 'not being able to be' and completes the idea of inexhaustibility below.
Eſgotar completes the definition as incapable of being exhausted. Mujin mugǔ reinforces this sense and is glossed as infinite.
Shuju mujinna koto wo yuu means saying an endless variety of things. The Portuguese va- begins varias, not a Japanese word.
Completes the translation as various things without limit. The short row belongs wholly to the preceding example.
Mujina is an animal name; the Portuguese places it among a kind of adibes. The historical comparison is retained without assigning a more precise modern species than the entry establishes.
Mujiki is being without food or not eating, explained by shoku nashi. The paragraph sign introduces the verbal example whose headword is divided after Mu-.
Mujiki wo suru means eating nothing. Ji in the first word continues the preceding Mu-; it is not a new entry.
Mujoo is impermanence, explained by tsune nashi. The visible descending j corrects OCR Muiǒ; the Portuguese emphasizes misery and the brevity of worldly things.

runs.text: das couſas do mundo. ¶ Item, Morrer.

lines.note: Completes the reference to worldly things, then adds the sense 'to die'. Mundo is chosen through an ink-blotted n-area on the evidence of its remaining strokes and the repeated mundo below, rather than OCR mugdo.
Mujoo no kaze ni sasowaruru pictures being drawn away by the wind of impermanence. The Portuguese interprets the image as being carried off by death and divides leuado at the margin.
Completes the death interpretation and begins ui mujoo no narai. Vy belongs to the Japanese phrase concerning the impermanence of conditioned or worldly things, not to the Portuguese apparatus.

runs.text: Custume das couſas do mundo q̃ ſe

lines.note: No narai completes the Japanese phrase for the ordinary course of worldly impermanence. The Portuguese says this is the custom of worldly things that change or end; q̃ remains abbreviated.
Completes the explanation: things readily come to an end or change. The faint open c supports acabão, not OCR a rabão; the historical nasal endings are retained.
This Mujǒ means supreme, explained by ue nashi, nothing above it. It is a distinct entry from impermanence; the visible caron is not replaced on etymological grounds.
Mujoo no sekki is directly glossed as death. The example repeats the expression with xec- divided before qi; no unprinted syllable is supplied from the stale reading hint.
Completes the example's expression for the time when one is driven or taken away by death. The historical passive/prospective ending raren is retained, and the Portuguese begins 'when we are'.
Completes the translation as being taken or summoned by death. The final upright S. identifies written usage.
Mujooson denotes the supreme holy or venerable one. Sancto preserves the historical Portuguese spelling, while the Japanese long s remains part of the roman headword.
Mujuu is without end, explained by owari nashi. Initial V in Vouari is the printed romanization, not a letter to modernize to O.
After completing 'without end', mushi, mujuu pairs absence of beginning with absence of ending. The Portuguese principio is divided after prin-.
Completes 'neither beginning nor end'. The stray mark above the blank area is not body text or an omitted word.

Mujun is explained by hoko and tate, spear and shield, but here glossed as enmity or fighting. The descending j in peleja agrees with Pelejar below and corrects OCR peleia; the modern abstract sense is not substituted for this gloss.
Mujun ni oyobu means coming to conflict, here fighting or quarrelling. Voyobu preserves the source's initial-v spelling.

runs.text: O não ter a Catana, ou Cogatana,

lines.note: Mumei concerns a sword or small blade lacking its maker's name or mark. Catana and Cogatana are Japanese object names embedded in the Portuguese definition, not independent headwords on this row.

runs.text: &c. nome, ou ſinal de quẽ a fez. ¶

lines.note: Completes the missing-maker's-mark definition. Co- begins the illustrative kono katana phrase on the following row; quẽ retains its printed abbreviation.
Kono katana wa mumei de gozaru says this sword is unsigned. The final Catana is embedded in the Portuguese translation, unlike catanaua in the Japanese example.

runs.text: não tem ſinal do official que a fez.

lines.note: Completes the statement that the blade has no mark of the craftsman who made it. Official here denotes the maker, not a government office.
Mumi means tasteless, explained by ajiwai nashi. The illustrative adjective is divided after Mu-, keeping the physical break.
Mumina koto describes something without taste or flavour. The Portuguese repeats the sensory meaning before the next row extends it to a person.
The figurative-use marker introduces mumina hito, an insipid person. Portuguese inſipido is divided after inſi-.
Completes the characterization as insipid and good for little. It belongs to the figurative human sense of Mumi.
Mumyoo is explained as lacking clarity. The Portuguese breaks claridade at the margin; the following homonym will instead concern absence of a name.
Completes 'without clarity, or a dark thing'. The written-language S. is upright, while the Portuguese explanation is italic.
This Mumyoo means nameless, explained by na nashi. The printed separation Na naxi is restored instead of OCR Nanaxi; the Portuguese repeats the absence of a name.
Completes 'a thing that has no name'. S. again labels written usage rather than contributing to the definition.
Mumon denotes lack of literacy or learning. Ichi- begins a proverb contrasting someone who knows a little with someone who knows nothing.

Ichimon wa mumon no shi nari says that one who knows a single written character can teach one who knows none. The n-area in xinari is worn; the apparent extra gap is not treated as a secure printed word space. The Portuguese starts 'one who knows one'.

runs.text: ſò letra, ou pouco, he mestre do que não ſabe

lines.note: Completes the first half of the comparison: knowing one letter, or a little, makes one a teacher of someone who knows nothing. The grave accent in ſò is retained.

runs.text: nada de letras. i, Na terra dos cegos o torto

lines.note: Closes the literal translation, then supplies the Portuguese proverb about the one-eyed person in the land of the blind. This is an explanatory analogy, not additional Japanese text.
Completes the proverb as 'is king'. The italic h, comparable with he above, corrects OCR be; the terminal S. remains a separate upright written-usage label.
